docs.text: MayaMetaBridge — User Guide 🇺🇸 English | 🇰🇷 한국어 MayaMetaBridge (MMB) brings Epic Games MetaHuman characters into Maya 2027: assemble one from its DNA files, drive the face, reshape the body, dress it, rig it with mGear, and send it out to Unreal Engine, Cascadeur, Marvelous Designer and ARKit. It is a port of the Blender add-on MetaBridge DNA — the same DNA files, the same RigLogic face rig, the same rules — reached through maya.cmds and OpenMaya. The panels, their rows and their buttons come from that add-on, so between the two guides the same panel is the same panel. The face above is the plug-in's own output: a MetaHuman assembled from head.dna and body.dna in a Maya 2027 viewport, wearing the maps from its own Maps folder. No stand-in render. What's new v0.1.0 — the Maya port Assemble — a MetaHuman folder in, a rigged, textured character out. In the reference character this guide's pictures come from: 1212 joints (870 in the head, 342 in the body) and 17 maps from its own Maps folder wired through 20 materials. The face board — Epic's own picker, built from the plug-in's own faceboard.json , so the dials are the ones the character expects. 124 of the add-on's 143 commands are ported, across all 18 panels and all 122 buttons those panels draw. The 19 that are not are the 18 panel ids plus one operator ( mmb_save_mat_defaults , see Limits ). Hair as an XGen groom — an Alembic groom comes in as one XGen interactive-groom description on the head (not a node per strand), with a guides / strands choice, a live preview you drag to line it up, and a bind that makes it follow the head. See Wearables . ARKit that matches the rig — head rotation about the world's axes, a Calibrate Neutral Face button, and the blink, tongue, cheek-puff and "oo" corrected against what the rig actually does. See ARKit Live . Body Blend, the add-on's way — a source list with thumbnails, a primary row, head blending, a character built into a registered slot, and a live preview; and Expression Presets as sliders that blend. See Body Blend . Arnold Look-Dev — the port's own scene to look at a character in: an Arnold twin of every material ( the XGen groom's hair included , which used to be the one part of a character the port could not shade), a five-light beauty rig with a sky dome, an 85 mm bust and a 50 mm full-figure camera, and the render settings a still is normally shot at - rendered on the GPU , with the CPU as the fallback. Two things Arnold's GPU cannot do are handled rather than discovered: a groom is given an aiStandardHair (Maya's own hairPhysicalShader has no GPU implementation at all, and MtoA answers that by crashing the whole session), and adaptive sampling is turned off for the GPU, because MtoA 5.6.2 crashes on it instead of refusing it. The press also exposes the rig , which is the difference between a lit character and a white blob: it renders a small probe of the face, reads the skin's own brightness in the display space the RenderView shows, and moves the rig (the sky dome included, since that is what lights a face here) until the lit cheek lands on the reference still's own measured skin - 0.59 median / 0.79 at its 75th percentile - while what the camera sees of the dome stays where the design put it, so the backdrop does not go dark with it. Measured on a real character, the design values read 1.00 in the face box and the press lands them at 0.61 / 0.78 with no clipped pixels, against the reference's 0.59 / 0.79 and a 0.84 backdrop. The three rows are in the main panel's Arnold Look-Dev (Maya-only) frame. mGear, one click — the port's own feature, not a port of anything: the Blender add-on rigs with Rigify, and Maya has mGear. The click places mGear's MetaHuman guide on the character's joints and builds the Shifter rig over it, then binds the head so the face follows the body. What is this plug-in? With it you can: Load a MetaHuman character (head + body) into Maya from its .dna files Move the face board's dials, or drive the face from an iPhone , live Save expressions as presets and blend several at once as sliders Reshape the body with proportion sliders — the DNA follows the sliders Blend several bodies into a new one Put clothing, hair and accessories on the character, and keep them on Build an animatable body rig with mGear , and retarget animation onto it Sculpt correctives on the skin and sync them to worn clothing Export everything back to DNA , FBX or glTF There is no N panel in Maya. The add-on draws eighteen panels down one sidebar; here each panel is a window of its own, and there are two ways to reach them: the MMB menu in Maya's menu bar, and the hub ( Show MMB Window ), which lists every panel and says how much of the port is done. Installing Unzip this folder anywhere you keep tools. The folder is used where it is — do not move it afterwards. Run the installer with Maya's Python (or any Python 3): python installer/install.py Add --maya-version 2027 if you have more than one Maya installed, and --remove to take it out again. 3. Restart Maya. The MMB menu appears in the menu bar. What the installer touches is one block in your Maya preferences — <prefs>/scripts/userSetup.py — which defers one loadPlugin to the first idle. Your previous userSetup.py is kept beside it as userSetup.py.bak-mmbb , and the block is replaced rather than appended, so running the installer twice is the same as running it once. It does not touch Maya.env , your modules folder, or anything else in the preferences. To load it for one session only, run this in the Script Editor: import maya.cmds as cmds cmds . loadPlugin ( r "<this folder>/mmb_plugin.py" ) Maya needs 2027 (Python 3.13), Windows 64-bit. The DNA and RigLogic libraries for Windows are bundled in mmb/lib , so nothing else has to be installed. The menu Eight entries and two dividers: the hub, then the six things a character actually needs, then All Panels . Assemble a MetaHuman opens the assembler rather than building straight away — the button that builds is in the panel, where the character to build is picked and where a click that would rebuild the character under you can say so instead. Under All Panels every panel is one item, grouped the way the hub's Pro view groups them: Character , Face & Animation , Body Rig & Sculpt , Live Links , Assets & Export . Each item opens that panel's own window; the menu does not draw its buttons a second time. The hub, and two views of it Show MMB Window opens the hub. Its first control is the view: Simple (left) is six numbered steps in the order the work happens — assemble, reshape, try on expressions, add clothing, record, export — and one button to the whole list. Pro (right) is all eighteen panels grouped by what they are for, each row saying how many buttons it holds. The line under the switch is the port's own progress — 18 panels, 122 buttons, 90 settings — 124 of 143 commands — and the view you leave it in is remembered. The port's windows are ordinary Maya windows: they dock where you drop them, and a saved Maya layout brings them back (each one restores through its own uiScript ). Two of them over the character: the assembler and the proportion sliders. This is the shape of a session — the character in the viewport, the panel you are working in beside it. Plug-ins for the other programs Four features reach into a program outside Maya, and each needs something on that side. Program What it is Needed for mGear your own install — put its scripts folder on MAYA_MODULE_PATH One-Click mGear Rig , the Anim Picker (§6) Cascadeur the third_party/MetaBridgeLive folder Send to Cascadeur (§13) Unreal Engine third_party/MotionForgeLiveLink , or downloaded on first use Unreal Live , Follow Unreal (§14) Marvelous Designer the mmb/md_plugin folder MD Live (§12) Cascadeur's and Marvelous Designer's plug-ins come with this package — nothing to download. The Unreal one is fetched from GitHub the first time you press Open Unreal Plug-in Folder ; needs an internet connection just that once. Install none of them to start with: each section below sets up its own when you get there. 1. Assembling a MetaHuman In MetaHumans Directory , pick the folder your MetaHumans live in — the one with head.dna inside. A folder is a character when it holds head.dna ; pointing at a character folder also lists that character's own siblings. Press Refresh Character List and pick the character. Leave Head , Body and Textures on. LOD chooses which mesh level to load — 0 is the fullest, and the only level the Bust slider works on (§5). Press Assemble . The character arrives as ordinary Maya nodes: a skeleton, skinned meshes with their materials wired to the Maps folder beside the DNA, and the face board (§2). Measured on the reference character this guide's pictures come from: 1212 joints (870 in the head part and 342 in the body), and 17 maps wired through 20 materials. Assembled Characters is the list of what is in the scene. Activate Slot makes one active (most of the rest of the plug-in works on the active slot), Toggle Face Rig shows or hides that character's face board, Delete Slot takes it out of the list, and Relink DNA re-points a slot at its DNA file after the file moved. Load Head DNA… and Load Body DNA… bring a single part in on its own. Two more things in the panel worth knowing: Re-Assemble is the same command as Assemble (it is there because a slot that drifted halfway through the work is the reason to press it), and the mGear Rig frame at the foot of the panel is §6. 2. The face board Assembling a MetaHuman leaves more in the scene than a rig: a face board (picker) beside the head, one control per facial expression. It is Epic's own board, not the port's invention — the plug-in builds it from the same faceboard.json its Maya plug-in uses (175 GUI controls and 3 analog ones, each with its shape, colour, limits and slider track), so a jaw you open here is the jaw the character's RigLogic expects. Dial values on the board are the interface everything else uses: ARKit Live (§4) drives them from your iPhone, Expression Presets (§3) save and reapply them, Animation Baker (§15) bakes them over the frame range, Pose Reset (§15) puts them back to neutral, and the RigLogic face rig evaluates them, which is what makes the skin move — there are no shape keys to edit. Toggle Face Rig (main panel, Face Rig frame) shows the board and hides it again. While the body is on a rig (§5 or §6) the head part follows it: a character whose head is not linked turns its face and not its head. The RNA list (main panel, RNA tab) lists the DNA's raw-control channels beside the control that drives each one. View switches between the DNA view (one row per channel: rc# , the channel, the connected control and Connect / Change / x ) and the Bone view (one row per control with its channels); Filter , Show (All / Mapped / Unmapped), Parent and Per Page narrow it and the list redraws as you change them, with < Prev / Next > for pages. Connect asks for a control and stores the mapping with the character; Clear All drops every manual mapping and puts the channels back on their own controls. A body-only DNA has no face channels, and the list says so. 3. Expression presets A preset is a JSON file of the face board's dial values, keyed by control name, so it travels between scenes and machines. Save Current Expression writes the board's current values over the preset picked in the list; Save As Current Expression… writes a new one. Apply Preset does not snap the face to that pose: it adds the preset to the slider list at 1.0 , and the face becomes the blend of every slider in that list. Two presets that open the same jaw do not add up past the bigger one — the blend takes the largest contribution per control. Add All From Active Folder adds every preset in the folder at 0.0 , so a folder becomes a bank of sliders you fade in. Clear All Sliders empties the list and puts the face back to neutral; Delete Expression Preset deletes the file; Set Folder… and Open Presets Folder work on the folder the presets live in. The ARKit presets ship with the plug-in : mmb/presets/ARKit , one ARKit_<name>.json per blendshape, with the name mapping beside them. That mapping is what ARKit Live (§4) drives. 4. ARKit Live — the iPhone's face Apple's Live Link Face app streams the 52 ARKit blendshapes over UDP as big-endian floats. The plug-in receives them on a background socket, and the scene is touched on the idle job — Maya's main thread. In Live Link Face, point the stream at this machine (the app's default port is 11111 , which is what the panel is set to). Host 0.0.0.0 takes the stream on every interface; change it to pin one. Connect . The face follows as you talk. Tune with Smoothing ( 0.5 ), Deadzone ( 0 ) and Gain ( 1.0 ), which are applied per blendshape exactly as the add-on applies them. Record records what is applied as keys; Load Live Link Face CSV… takes the app's own recording instead (one row per frame), and Export Face CSV… writes the current face out the same way. Export ARKit Blend Shapes (FBX)… writes an ARKit-named blendshape set as FBX for other tools, and Rebuild Name Mapping rebuilds the mapping between ARKit names and the board's controls when a character arrives with a naming that does not match. Head Rotation (Experimental) turns the character's head from the phone's head pose: pitch nods about the world's X, yaw turns about Y and roll tilts about Z, on top of the head's own orientation. Use Invert Pitch / Yaw / Roll if a direction is the wrong way round for the way the phone is held. Calibrate Neutral Face — a phone never reads a relaxed face as zero: the mouth-shrug, roll and stretch shapes each sit at 0.1–0.3 and together open the mouth a little, and a relaxed eye reads as eyeWide 0.4. Relax, mouth closed, eyes as you normally hold them, and press it: the average of a second of frames becomes the resting face, every shape is measured from it, and a slightly narrower eye (a smaller eyeWide ) now closes the lids a little instead of being lost. Clear Neutral Calibration forgets it. It is kept with the settings. Four shapes are corrected for this rig, because the add-on's presets and the board's DNA put some controls the other way round (36 channels, among them the blink and the tongue's in/out): the blink closes the lids and eyeWide opens them, tongueOut puts the tongue out, cheekPuff blows the cheeks with the lips sealed (the preset also blew the lips forward), and mouthPucker narrows the mouth through the corner controls so an "oo" reads as one. 5. Proportions Eighteen sliders, all factors on the character as it was built, with 1.0 being that character. A slider that moves moves the character — there is no Apply button, the same as in the add-on. Group Slider Range Length Leg Length 0.80 – 1.30 Length Torso Length 0.85 – 1.20 Length Neck Length 0.80 – 1.30 Length Arm Length 0.85 – 1.20 Width Shoulder Width 0.85 – 1.20 Width Hip Width 0.85 – 1.20 Width Waist 0.75 – 1.30 Width Chest 0.80 – 1.25 Width Hips 0.80 – 1.25 Width Thigh 0.75 – 1.30 Width Calf 0.75 – 1.30 Width Upper Arm 0.75 – 1.30 Width Forearm 0.75 – 1.30 Width Neck Thickness 0.80 – 1.25 Shape Bust 0.50 – 1.50 — needs the LOD 0 body Size Head Size 0.90 – 1.10 Shoes Heel Height 0 – 15 cm Shoes Front Height 0 – 5 cm What the sliders do, and what they deliberately do not: lengths stretch a segment by moving the joint at its end, never by scaling a bone — a longer thigh is not a fatter one; widths move the joint the width is measured at, and the hip keeps only its left-right offset scaled; the whole body rides with the feet, so longer legs lift the character instead of pushing the soles through the floor; the skin follows through its own skinning , which is what a Maya character does when its joints move, and the mesh fields (girths, bust, shoes, head) come on top of the same bone moves; every change is worked out from the rest skeleton again , so nothing drifts and setting a slider back to 1.0 gives the original character back exactly. Long Legs sets the one-click look the add-on has; Reset puts every slider back. Two things the panel says and means: assemble a character with a body first, and if a control rig (§6) is standing over the character, remove it before reshaping and build it again afterwards. 6. The body rig — mGear, one click The character's own skeleton — 1212 joints — which any body rig is built over. The same character on the rig the one click builds. This is the port's own feature. The Blender add-on rigs with Rigify ; Maya has mGear , and a MetaHuman user already has it installed — so the click places mGear's own MetaHuman guide on the character's joints and builds mGear's Shifter rig over it. Put mGear's scripts folder on MAYA_MODULE_PATH first. Then, in the main panel's mGear Rig (Maya-only) frame: Button What it does One-Click mGear Rig snap the guide onto the character, build the rig, and bind the head Snap mGear Guide put the guide's locators back on the joints, for a guide you moved by hand Bind Head to mGear Rig constrain the head part to the body joints mGear drives (the one-click does this already) Unbind Head from mGear Rig take those constraints out again; the head keeps its values where it stands Register Anim Picker make mGear's Anim Picker for the rig — body and face pages — and open it Remove mGear Rig delete the guide and the rigs; the character stays as it is Two details the plug-in reports rather than hides: a guide locator whose joint the character does not have is left where the template put it (and the console says which), and a MetaHuman is two skeletons that share joint names — the neck's, among others — so the other part's joints are given names of their own while mGear connects and their own names back afterwards. The add-on's own rig buttons The Rigify Body Control Rig frame in the main panel is the add-on's rig workflow, and in Maya it builds a Maya control rig over the character's key joints (the add-on's two steps, 1. Build Meta-Rig and 2. Generate Control Rig , then 3. Apply Retarget so the character follows it). Alongside them: Remove Retarget / Remove Control Rig take it back out; Link Head Rig / Unlink Head Rig attach the head part, which is what makes the face follow the body; Toggle RBF Correctives (Body) , Driver Bone , Show RBF Controls / Hide — the add-on's RBF corrective pass and its manual controls; Import FBX Animation… imports animation onto the rig; Toggle IK Stretch , Toggle Heel Pivot , Toggle Finger IK , IK to FK / FK to IK , Snap Fingertip Targets — the limb and finger switches, including the per-finger 0 = joints, 1 = fingertip blend. Retargeting an animation from another rig is its own panel — §15. 7. Body Blend Several bodies averaged into one new character. A source row is either a body DNA file (with the head DNA that goes with it) or one archetype of a library file, and each has a weight. One row is the primary — the highlighted one — and it has to be a real DNA file, because a library entry carries no RigLogic data of its own: the primary is what the new character's rig is built from. Use Base DNA adds the bundled reference Body.dna (and Head.dna ) as the primary row; Add Body DNA / Add Folder… add files at weight 0 ; Load Library… adds a library's archetypes at 0 ; Export… writes a library file out. Build Blended Body averages the rows that carry weight — body and, when every one of them has head data, head too — and builds a new character in the slot list. Blend Active Character applies the blend to the character you already have instead, and Replace chooses between adding and replacing. Live Preview is off by default: it is the switch that makes a weight drag show its result while you drag. 8. Wearables — clothing and hair Import Clothing (FBX)… brings a garment in (and Head Accessory… the same for something that goes on the head). Make Garment Rig , then Bind Garment To Character — binding copies the body's skin weights onto the piece, so it moves the way the skin beneath it moves. Fit to the skin keeps a garment out of the character's body. A garment modelled over another build sinks into this one wherever the two differ; the fit finds, for every vertex, the nearest point of the body and head skin, and one that is inside it - or closer than the offset - is moved out along the skin's normal. Nothing else moves, so loose cloth stays loose, and a point that only slides along the skin is left alone. Fit Clothing to Skin (the Fit to Skin frame) fits the selected garment - or everything worn when nothing is selected. It also runs by itself on Bind Garment To Character and on Refit . Clothing Offset (0–0.02, the add-on's metres: 0.01 is one centimetre) is the gap left between cloth and skin; the minimum is 0.2 cm, and moving the slider refits what is worn straight away. The fit always starts from the garment as it was first seen, so a smaller offset lets the cloth come back out. A point deeper than 8 cm inside the skin is taken for another surface (an arm behind the torso) and is not pulled across. On a skinned garment the fit is written to the rest shape the skin cluster reads, so it stays when the character moves. Refit Clothing To Body re-applies the proportions' girth field to everything worn, so a changed waist changes the clothes over it too - and then fits the result to the skin with the Clothing Offset. Hair is a separate road, and it is an XGen interactive groom : Import Hair… (Alembic) reads the file as data and makes one XGen spline description on the character's head mesh - no node per strand (a MetaHuman groom has hundreds of thousands, which is what took Maya down when the file was imported the ordinary way). The groom's Z-up is turned to Maya's Y-up. Import chooses Guides + Strands , Strands only or Guides only . A file written by a groom exporter marks each curve ( groom_guide ), so the three really differ; a file without that mark is all strands. Hair Strands (0 = all) limits how many are built. XGen evaluates about 1.4 ms a strand, so the default of 10,000 is a few seconds; raise it for a finished groom. Line it up by eye. XGen holds a groom's own node at identity, so moving it does nothing. The import gives a locator, MMB_Hair_…_move , and a light preview of 250 strands under it: drag it and the preview follows at once. Nothing is written on release - the placement is applied by the press that seats the groom ( Bind , Retarget , Apply Hair Offset / Scale ), so lining hair up stays a drag and not a wait. Picking the hair picks the locator for you. Align Active Mesh to DNA Head seats the groom's roots on the head's surface : the mean vector from each root to the nearest point of the character mesh, iterated, all three axes of it, and the answer carries the measurement (the roots' mean and worst distance to the surface, before and after). It used to be a bounding box - the groom's control centred on the character mesh's box in X and Z, the height left alone - and measured on the sample guide groom over the bundled body that took the roots further from the head: 13.23 units off the surface before the button, 17.34 after. The surface fit takes the same groom, deliberately slid by (12, 15, -9) , from 20.14 back to 2.52 - and a groom that is already seated is left alone, because a step is only taken when it measures better. Hair Offset X/Y/Z , Hair Scale and Apply Hair Offset / Scale place it by number instead, and the numbers are absolute : the button puts the locator at the groom's own centre plus the offset (uniform scale from Hair Scale ) and writes the file in that same press, so it does not add to a hand drag - a groom lined up by eye returns to centre plus offset. What that buys is repeatability: the same numbers give the same placement in any scene. Bind Hair To Head re-seats the groom on the head mesh, so it follows the skin and Body Blend (a hair mesh or curves are constrained to the head joint instead). The light strand display the import made stays - it is the visible hair, and it is moved onto the head joint with the rest, so it follows the skin too. (It used to be deleted here, which is why the curves seemed to vanish on bind.) Retarget Hair to Selected Mesh does the same onto another mesh: select the hair, then the mesh. Sculpt brushes (Comb, Grab, Length, Smooth…) work on the groom. Density and Place are a different matter : they paint how strands are generated , and an imported groom is the file's own strands - measured, its density mask, its multiplier and its interpolation move 2745 splines not at all, and two renders of the same frame differ in 0 of 864000 bytes. There is no XGen grooming conversion, and the panel no longer offers one. Maya 2027 cannot turn an Alembic groom into XGen's own spline or guide data: the only ABC path is a spline modifier that streams the file ( xgmCurveToSpline ), so the description holds no splines of its own and the ABC has to travel with the scene. Measured here: the reader keeps the file open, and Epic's own groom exporter refuses a spline description ( Must select either palette or description ) - it is built for classic descriptions only, and that path crashed this Maya in the batch test. The buttons that grew a second, classic description out of the curves ( Create XGen Groom , Apply Hair Length , Apply Hair Width , Write Groom Collection , Bake Hair for Render ) were therefore taken out of the panel: they did not convert the imported hair, they made a different one. What the port does instead is what XGen supports - import, place, bind, and groom with the interactive brushes, whose edits are sculpt layers on top of the file's splines. Place first, bind once. Dragging MMB_Hair_…_move moves the stand-in curves only; the groom's Alembic is written by the press that says where it belongs - Bind Hair To Head , Retarget Hair to Selected Mesh , Apply Hair Offset / Scale or Align Active Mesh to DNA Head . Those place the groom where it was dragged and then seat it. Re-writing the file on every drag release was the seconds-long stall the stand-in was invented for. Deleting the character takes its hair with it. An imported groom is a scene root of its own - XGen makes it beside the mesh, and the placement locator beside that - so removing a character used to leave the groom, its locator and its 250 stand-in curves floating over nothing. The character's record now carries its hair, so all three go with it. 9. Live corrective sculpting (Beta) The add-on's workflow, translated: sculpt the skin in a pose, and keep the difference as a named corrective that comes back with that pose. Name the corrective ( Corrective ), and give it the bone it hangs off for a face ( Head Bone ) or a body ( Body Driver Bone ) pass. Begin (Face) or Begin (Body) takes a baseline: the mesh as it stands and the pose that stands with it. Sculpt the vertices — the port's delta is taken against that baseline. Finish Sculpt stores the difference, sparse and named, on the character. Edit Sculpt loads a stored corrective back for another pass, Set Neutral re-keys the pose it hangs off, Toggle Manual Override marks it always-on, and Remove Corrective deletes it. Sync to Wearables carries the applied difference onto worn garments through the same nearest-vertex map the garment bind uses. Bake Corrective to DNA writes it into the DNA file; Write to DNA (head only) ( Export Edited Shape Keys ) and Bake All to DNA do the same for a batch. A DNA key you sculpted yourself — jaw_open , say — replaces that channel when you press Export Edited Shape Keys . Export… and Import… move the whole registry as JSON. The deltas are the data; everything else in the panel is bookkeeping around them. 10. Exporting Head and Body write the active slot's DNA, through the library's own writer, read back as proof. Export FBX writes the character through the FBX plug-in; Export glTF through Maya's glTF translator. With no path given, a file dialog asks. The Save Head / Save Body DNA commands are the same two files with a suggested name — <source stem>_export.dna , beside the DNA it was read from — and with the Include Mesh Edits question answered: what Proportions (§5) and Sculpt (§9) did lives on the Maya skeleton and mesh, and the writer patches those edits into the file the character came from, so the DNA is the character on screen. Lower LODs follow the nearest LOD-0 vertex, or they would keep the unedited shape and pop in the distance. If the mesh edits cannot be written, the port says so loudly instead of writing a file that quietly dropped them. Export All Slots (§11) does the DNA export for every slot in the list. 11. DNA validation and batch tools Validate DNA File… reads a .dna and reports what is wrong with it; Validate Active Slot does the same for the character you are working on, so a file that will not assemble is a sentence before the pipeline meets it rather than a stack trace later. Batch Tools is two buttons: Assemble All Characters (every character in the folder the plug-in is pointed at) and Export All Slots (the DNA of every slot in the scene). 12. MD Live — Marvelous Designer Plain files in one shared folder , and the plug-in that ships in mmb/md_plugin . Maya → MD: Send Body to MD writes an avatar .obj into the shared folder ( Send Scale , Include Head and Prepare for Auto-Fit decide what goes in it). In Marvelous Designer, add the scripts from the plug-in folder in Plug-in > Plug-in Manager — maya_live.py for Live , and maya_load_avatar.py / maya_send_garment.py for a one-shot round trip — and run the one you need. Open MD Plug-in Folder opens that folder for you. MD → Maya: the garment lands in the same folder. Get Garment Now imports the newest one, Import Garment from MD… picks a file by hand, and Live watches the folder on idle and imports the moment a garment lands, so the round trip is one click on each side. Buttons and zippers are dropped, the avatar and lean copies are excluded, and units are honoured through the plug-in's own .mayaunits.json . Merge Pattern Pieces chooses between the patterns as cut and one welded mesh; Wear As is the category the garment is worn as, and Sim Steps / Auto Return tune what the round trip does. 13. Send to Cascadeur Two localhost ports, MetaBridge Live's own: 9584 receives characters and poses, 9586 is the live link. They are not the ports any other Cascadeur bridge uses, so it can run beside one. Nothing leaves the machine. Press Install Cascadeur Plug-in once. The plug-in - MetaBridge Live , two files - ships in third_party/MetaBridgeLive ; Cascadeur keeps its scripts inside its own installation, which usually needs Administrator rights — the installer does the copy through a short-lived helper and reports what happened, and says so when the prompt is refused rather than half-installing. Choose what to send: Send ( Character and Bones or Keyframes Only ), Send Head , Face Bones , Send Anim , Append , Frame Rate . Press Send to Cascadeur (the whole scene, opens as a new scene in Cascadeur) or Current Frame (one frame, over the top from frame 0). Restart Cascadeur, then run Animation Scripts > MetaBridge Live once per session (run it again to stop). Cascadeur Status answers whether it is listening. Live: Mirror This Rig sends frames while you animate, and Stop Mirroring stops; Live Way and Live Bones choose what a mirrored frame carries. Send the character first, then go live. Clothes go with the character. Every mesh skinned to the character's joints (what Bind Garment recorded, and anything else bound to the rig) leaves in the same FBX and follows the pose in Cascadeur. A garment is re-skinned on a copy from the body and the head under it - so a hood follows the head and a baggy leg follows its own leg - and the original is not touched; the head's own neck and shoulder collar takes the body's weights, so the head stays joined at the neck. Send the character in its rest pose and let the pose follow (a character sent while posed can tear its clothes in Cascadeur). A coat with 170,000 vertices takes about half a minute. The character leaves as one skeleton - the head part's meshes are rebound to its body joints - and a take read back lands on both parts: the head's own copy of the body chain ( spine_04 up to head , the clavicles and the upperarms, at the body's exact rest transforms) is written from the body joints of the same name, so the head and its face ride along instead of standing in their rest pose. A character with no head part beside it is unaffected, and so is the face itself, which keeps being driven by the DNA's rig logic. 14. Unreal Engine Out (9561) — press Open Unreal Plug-in Folder once; it fetches MotionForgeLiveLink from GitHub the first time, and you copy it into your project's Plugins folder and restart the editor. In Unreal's Live Link window add the MotionForge source (port 9561); in the character Blueprint keep Use Live Link off . Then Start Unreal Live streams the face as you work — the same RigLogic runs on both sides, so only control values cross, one small frame per tick at the Rate you set. Mirror chooses what the stream carries. In (9562) — Follow Unreal makes this character follow a MetaHuman Unreal is animating: Host , Port , Rate , Body and Face decide what follows, and each frame's per-joint turns and offsets are applied as a delta from the rest pose captured when the follow began — and put back when it stops. Run MotionForge.Send.Start in Unreal first. 15. Animation baker, pose reset, preset converter, retarget Animation Baker — keyframe the face board's controls, then Bake Face Animation over the frame range; Clear Baked Animation takes the bake out again. (The panel's own line says the order: key the board first, then bake.) Pose Reset — Reset All Controls puts the whole face board back to neutral, Reset Selected only the controls you have selected, which is the one you want in the middle of a pose. External Preset Converter — a foreign preset names bones ; the board names controls , so the two are matched through a name_mapping.json . Convert & Import (Maya/Houdini)… brings a preset in from those tools and Convert ARKit Payload… from an ARKit payload; Edit Name Mapping opens the mapping to fill the empty targets before a re-import. Retarget Rigify Animation — bring animation from another rig onto this character. Source Type picks the profile — fifteen of them, from Auto Detect , UE5 Mannequin , Fortnite , MetaHuman , Mixamo and Rigify to SMPL-X , SOMA and Unitree G1 — Source Rig / Target Rig point at the two rigs, and Quality chooses the solve: Precise (floor + legs on IK) , Balanced (legs on IK) or Fast (rotations only) . Under the add-on's rows is the port's own frame, Retarget in Maya (HumanIK / mGear) , and it is where the take lands: Retarget Onto — the character's own joints (the solve keyed on the character's skeleton: rest poses aligned, root travel scaled, feet on IK, floor matched), HumanIK (Maya) (both rigs defined as HIK characters and Maya's own retarget baked), or the one-click mGear Controls . Target Type picks which rig on the character side the solve uses, Legs on IK keeps the feet on the floor rather than rotating them, and Source Rest Frame is the frame of the source take that stands as the rest pose ( -1 lets the solver work it out). Quick tips Anything a panel does, a command does. Every button is a Maya runtime command: cmds.mmb_mh_assemble() from the Script Editor, a MEL script or a shelf button. Maya's own tooltip on a button says which add-on feature it stands for and whether the work behind it is ported; the command's own name is beside each button in the Panel Reference . Settings are optionVars , prefixed mmb. , named after the add-on's property (the Textures checkbox is mmb.ml_mh_load_textures ). They survive a restart and can be set from MEL: optionVar -iv "mmb.ml_mh_load_textures" 0; From Python , mmb.api is the facade: import mmb.api as api api . status () # how much of the add-on is ported api . panels () # the eighteen panels, in sidebar order api . window () # open the hub api . run ( "mmb_mh_assemble" ) # run one button - Batch hosts : anything that needs a window refuses in mayapy and says so; the work that does not — assembling, exporting to a path you give, validating, baking — runs there, which is how the port's own test suite runs it ( tests/run_tests.py ). - Nothing is hidden in the scene : a character is a group of ordinary joints and meshes, the slot list is one network node ( MMB_Slots ) holding the data, and every setting is an optionVar — so a scene saved by the plug-in opens in any Maya, with or without the plug-in loaded. Limits of the port 124 of the add-on's 143 commands are implemented. The 19 that are not are the 18 panel ids (the add-on's panel classes, which have no Maya counterpart — the port draws its own windows) and mmb_save_mat_defaults , Save Material as Default : it would capture Blender's Principled BSDF socket values, and the port's materials are Arnold standardSurface nodes whose attribute names are entirely different — and nothing in the port reads such a file yet, so writing one would be a button that produces a file nobody reads. (Reload Materials and Reset Material Defaults are there and work.)* The plug-in's own checking happens out loud : a command that cannot do its work prints why in the Script Editor and, where it can, says it in the viewport, rather than changing nothing. The Cascadeur elevated install — the copy into a Program Files Cascadeur — is implemented and its planning half is tested, but the elevation half has not been run against a real installation of that kind. Report what happens if you use it. This guide's screenshots come from Maya 2027 on Windows, with the reference MetaHuman. Menu wording and window decoration differ on other systems; the panels are the same panels. Panel Reference Every panel, what it is for, and every control it draws — generated from the plug-in's own registry: Panel Reference (English) 패널 레퍼런스 (한국어)
docs.title: Welcome to MayaMetaBridge

docs.text: 🇺🇸 English | 🇰🇷 한국어 MayaMetaBridge (MMB) brings Epic Games MetaHuman characters into Maya 2027: assemble one from its DNA files, drive the face, reshape the body, dress it, rig it with mGear, and send it out to Unreal Engine, Cascadeur, Marvelous Designer and ARKit. It is a port of the Blender add-on MetaBridge DNA — the same DNA files, the same RigLogic face rig, the same rules — reached through maya.cmds and OpenMaya. The panels, their rows and their buttons come from that add-on, so between the two guides the same panel is the same panel. The face above is the plug-in's own output: a MetaHuman assembled from head.dna and body.dna in a Maya 2027 viewport, wearing the maps from its own Maps folder. No stand-in render.
docs.title: MayaMetaBridge — User Guide

docs.text: v0.1.0 — the Maya port Assemble — a MetaHuman folder in, a rigged, textured character out. In the reference character this guide's pictures come from: 1212 joints (870 in the head, 342 in the body) and 17 maps from its own Maps folder wired through 20 materials. The face board — Epic's own picker, built from the plug-in's own faceboard.json , so the dials are the ones the character expects. 124 of the add-on's 143 commands are ported, across all 18 panels and all 122 buttons those panels draw. The 19 that are not are the 18 panel ids plus one operator ( mmb_save_mat_defaults , see Limits ). Hair as an XGen groom — an Alembic groom comes in as one XGen interactive-groom description on the head (not a node per strand), with a guides / strands choice, a live preview you drag to line it up, and a bind that makes it follow the head. See Wearables . ARKit that matches the rig — head rotation about the world's axes, a Calibrate Neutral Face button, and the blink, tongue, cheek-puff and "oo" corrected against what the rig actually does. See ARKit Live . Body Blend, the add-on's way — a source list with thumbnails, a primary row, head blending, a character built into a registered slot, and a live preview; and Expression Presets as sliders that blend. See Body Blend . Arnold Look-Dev — the port's own scene to look at a character in: an Arnold twin of every material ( the XGen groom's hair included , which used to be the one part of a character the port could not shade), a five-light beauty rig with a sky dome, an 85 mm bust and a 50 mm full-figure camera, and the render settings a still is normally shot at - rendered on the GPU , with the CPU as the fallback. Two things Arnold's GPU cannot do are handled rather than discovered: a groom is given an aiStandardHair (Maya's own hairPhysicalShader has no GPU implementation at all, and MtoA answers that by crashing the whole session), and adaptive sampling is turned off for the GPU, because MtoA 5.6.2 crashes on it instead of refusing it. The press also exposes the rig , which is the difference between a lit character and a white blob: it renders a small probe of the face, reads the skin's own brightness in the display space the RenderView shows, and moves the rig (the sky dome included, since that is what lights a face here) until the lit cheek lands on the reference still's own measured skin - 0.59 median / 0.79 at its 75th percentile - while what the camera sees of the dome stays where the design put it, so the backdrop does not go dark with it. Measured on a real character, the design values read 1.00 in the face box and the press lands them at 0.61 / 0.78 with no clipped pixels, against the reference's 0.59 / 0.79 and a 0.84 backdrop. The three rows are in the main panel's Arnold Look-Dev (Maya-only) frame. mGear, one click — the port's own feature, not a port of anything: the Blender add-on rigs with Rigify, and Maya has mGear. The click places mGear's MetaHuman guide on the character's joints and builds the Shifter rig over it, then binds the head so the face follows the body.
docs.title: What's new

docs.text: With it you can: Load a MetaHuman character (head + body) into Maya from its .dna files Move the face board's dials, or drive the face from an iPhone , live Save expressions as presets and blend several at once as sliders Reshape the body with proportion sliders — the DNA follows the sliders Blend several bodies into a new one Put clothing, hair and accessories on the character, and keep them on Build an animatable body rig with mGear , and retarget animation onto it Sculpt correctives on the skin and sync them to worn clothing Export everything back to DNA , FBX or glTF There is no N panel in Maya. The add-on draws eighteen panels down one sidebar; here each panel is a window of its own, and there are two ways to reach them: the MMB menu in Maya's menu bar, and the hub ( Show MMB Window ), which lists every panel and says how much of the port is done.
docs.title: What is this plug-in?

docs.text: Unzip this folder anywhere you keep tools. The folder is used where it is — do not move it afterwards. Run the installer with Maya's Python (or any Python 3): python installer/install.py Add --maya-version 2027 if you have more than one Maya installed, and --remove to take it out again. 3. Restart Maya. The MMB menu appears in the menu bar. What the installer touches is one block in your Maya preferences — <prefs>/scripts/userSetup.py — which defers one loadPlugin to the first idle. Your previous userSetup.py is kept beside it as userSetup.py.bak-mmbb , and the block is replaced rather than appended, so running the installer twice is the same as running it once. It does not touch Maya.env , your modules folder, or anything else in the preferences. To load it for one session only, run this in the Script Editor: import maya.cmds as cmds cmds . loadPlugin ( r "<this folder>/mmb_plugin.py" ) Maya needs 2027 (Python 3.13), Windows 64-bit. The DNA and RigLogic libraries for Windows are bundled in mmb/lib , so nothing else has to be installed.
docs.title: Installing

docs.text: Eight entries and two dividers: the hub, then the six things a character actually needs, then All Panels . Assemble a MetaHuman opens the assembler rather than building straight away — the button that builds is in the panel, where the character to build is picked and where a click that would rebuild the character under you can say so instead. Under All Panels every panel is one item, grouped the way the hub's Pro view groups them: Character , Face & Animation , Body Rig & Sculpt , Live Links , Assets & Export . Each item opens that panel's own window; the menu does not draw its buttons a second time.
docs.title: The menu

docs.text: Show MMB Window opens the hub. Its first control is the view: Simple (left) is six numbered steps in the order the work happens — assemble, reshape, try on expressions, add clothing, record, export — and one button to the whole list. Pro (right) is all eighteen panels grouped by what they are for, each row saying how many buttons it holds. The line under the switch is the port's own progress — 18 panels, 122 buttons, 90 settings — 124 of 143 commands — and the view you leave it in is remembered. The port's windows are ordinary Maya windows: they dock where you drop them, and a saved Maya layout brings them back (each one restores through its own uiScript ). Two of them over the character: the assembler and the proportion sliders. This is the shape of a session — the character in the viewport, the panel you are working in beside it.
docs.title: The hub, and two views of it

docs.text: Four features reach into a program outside Maya, and each needs something on that side. Program What it is Needed for mGear your own install — put its scripts folder on MAYA_MODULE_PATH One-Click mGear Rig , the Anim Picker (§6) Cascadeur the third_party/MetaBridgeLive folder Send to Cascadeur (§13) Unreal Engine third_party/MotionForgeLiveLink , or downloaded on first use Unreal Live , Follow Unreal (§14) Marvelous Designer the mmb/md_plugin folder MD Live (§12) Cascadeur's and Marvelous Designer's plug-ins come with this package — nothing to download. The Unreal one is fetched from GitHub the first time you press Open Unreal Plug-in Folder ; needs an internet connection just that once. Install none of them to start with: each section below sets up its own when you get there.
docs.title: Plug-ins for the other programs

docs.text: In MetaHumans Directory , pick the folder your MetaHumans live in — the one with head.dna inside. A folder is a character when it holds head.dna ; pointing at a character folder also lists that character's own siblings. Press Refresh Character List and pick the character. Leave Head , Body and Textures on. LOD chooses which mesh level to load — 0 is the fullest, and the only level the Bust slider works on (§5). Press Assemble . The character arrives as ordinary Maya nodes: a skeleton, skinned meshes with their materials wired to the Maps folder beside the DNA, and the face board (§2). Measured on the reference character this guide's pictures come from: 1212 joints (870 in the head part and 342 in the body), and 17 maps wired through 20 materials. Assembled Characters is the list of what is in the scene. Activate Slot makes one active (most of the rest of the plug-in works on the active slot), Toggle Face Rig shows or hides that character's face board, Delete Slot takes it out of the list, and Relink DNA re-points a slot at its DNA file after the file moved. Load Head DNA… and Load Body DNA… bring a single part in on its own. Two more things in the panel worth knowing: Re-Assemble is the same command as Assemble (it is there because a slot that drifted halfway through the work is the reason to press it), and the mGear Rig frame at the foot of the panel is §6.
docs.title: 1. Assembling a MetaHuman

docs.text: Assembling a MetaHuman leaves more in the scene than a rig: a face board (picker) beside the head, one control per facial expression. It is Epic's own board, not the port's invention — the plug-in builds it from the same faceboard.json its Maya plug-in uses (175 GUI controls and 3 analog ones, each with its shape, colour, limits and slider track), so a jaw you open here is the jaw the character's RigLogic expects. Dial values on the board are the interface everything else uses: ARKit Live (§4) drives them from your iPhone, Expression Presets (§3) save and reapply them, Animation Baker (§15) bakes them over the frame range, Pose Reset (§15) puts them back to neutral, and the RigLogic face rig evaluates them, which is what makes the skin move — there are no shape keys to edit. Toggle Face Rig (main panel, Face Rig frame) shows the board and hides it again. While the body is on a rig (§5 or §6) the head part follows it: a character whose head is not linked turns its face and not its head. The RNA list (main panel, RNA tab) lists the DNA's raw-control channels beside the control that drives each one. View switches between the DNA view (one row per channel: rc# , the channel, the connected control and Connect / Change / x ) and the Bone view (one row per control with its channels); Filter , Show (All / Mapped / Unmapped), Parent and Per Page narrow it and the list redraws as you change them, with < Prev / Next > for pages. Connect asks for a control and stores the mapping with the character; Clear All drops every manual mapping and puts the channels back on their own controls. A body-only DNA has no face channels, and the list says so.
docs.title: 2. The face board

docs.text: A preset is a JSON file of the face board's dial values, keyed by control name, so it travels between scenes and machines. Save Current Expression writes the board's current values over the preset picked in the list; Save As Current Expression… writes a new one. Apply Preset does not snap the face to that pose: it adds the preset to the slider list at 1.0 , and the face becomes the blend of every slider in that list. Two presets that open the same jaw do not add up past the bigger one — the blend takes the largest contribution per control. Add All From Active Folder adds every preset in the folder at 0.0 , so a folder becomes a bank of sliders you fade in. Clear All Sliders empties the list and puts the face back to neutral; Delete Expression Preset deletes the file; Set Folder… and Open Presets Folder work on the folder the presets live in. The ARKit presets ship with the plug-in : mmb/presets/ARKit , one ARKit_<name>.json per blendshape, with the name mapping beside them. That mapping is what ARKit Live (§4) drives.
docs.title: 3. Expression presets

docs.text: Apple's Live Link Face app streams the 52 ARKit blendshapes over UDP as big-endian floats. The plug-in receives them on a background socket, and the scene is touched on the idle job — Maya's main thread. In Live Link Face, point the stream at this machine (the app's default port is 11111 , which is what the panel is set to). Host 0.0.0.0 takes the stream on every interface; change it to pin one. Connect . The face follows as you talk. Tune with Smoothing ( 0.5 ), Deadzone ( 0 ) and Gain ( 1.0 ), which are applied per blendshape exactly as the add-on applies them. Record records what is applied as keys; Load Live Link Face CSV… takes the app's own recording instead (one row per frame), and Export Face CSV… writes the current face out the same way. Export ARKit Blend Shapes (FBX)… writes an ARKit-named blendshape set as FBX for other tools, and Rebuild Name Mapping rebuilds the mapping between ARKit names and the board's controls when a character arrives with a naming that does not match. Head Rotation (Experimental) turns the character's head from the phone's head pose: pitch nods about the world's X, yaw turns about Y and roll tilts about Z, on top of the head's own orientation. Use Invert Pitch / Yaw / Roll if a direction is the wrong way round for the way the phone is held. Calibrate Neutral Face — a phone never reads a relaxed face as zero: the mouth-shrug, roll and stretch shapes each sit at 0.1–0.3 and together open the mouth a little, and a relaxed eye reads as eyeWide 0.4. Relax, mouth closed, eyes as you normally hold them, and press it: the average of a second of frames becomes the resting face, every shape is measured from it, and a slightly narrower eye (a smaller eyeWide ) now closes the lids a little instead of being lost. Clear Neutral Calibration forgets it. It is kept with the settings. Four shapes are corrected for this rig, because the add-on's presets and the board's DNA put some controls the other way round (36 channels, among them the blink and the tongue's in/out): the blink closes the lids and eyeWide opens them, tongueOut puts the tongue out, cheekPuff blows the cheeks with the lips sealed (the preset also blew the lips forward), and mouthPucker narrows the mouth through the corner controls so an "oo" reads as one.
docs.title: 4. ARKit Live — the iPhone's face

docs.text: Eighteen sliders, all factors on the character as it was built, with 1.0 being that character. A slider that moves moves the character — there is no Apply button, the same as in the add-on. Group Slider Range Length Leg Length 0.80 – 1.30 Length Torso Length 0.85 – 1.20 Length Neck Length 0.80 – 1.30 Length Arm Length 0.85 – 1.20 Width Shoulder Width 0.85 – 1.20 Width Hip Width 0.85 – 1.20 Width Waist 0.75 – 1.30 Width Chest 0.80 – 1.25 Width Hips 0.80 – 1.25 Width Thigh 0.75 – 1.30 Width Calf 0.75 – 1.30 Width Upper Arm 0.75 – 1.30 Width Forearm 0.75 – 1.30 Width Neck Thickness 0.80 – 1.25 Shape Bust 0.50 – 1.50 — needs the LOD 0 body Size Head Size 0.90 – 1.10 Shoes Heel Height 0 – 15 cm Shoes Front Height 0 – 5 cm What the sliders do, and what they deliberately do not: lengths stretch a segment by moving the joint at its end, never by scaling a bone — a longer thigh is not a fatter one; widths move the joint the width is measured at, and the hip keeps only its left-right offset scaled; the whole body rides with the feet, so longer legs lift the character instead of pushing the soles through the floor; the skin follows through its own skinning , which is what a Maya character does when its joints move, and the mesh fields (girths, bust, shoes, head) come on top of the same bone moves; every change is worked out from the rest skeleton again , so nothing drifts and setting a slider back to 1.0 gives the original character back exactly. Long Legs sets the one-click look the add-on has; Reset puts every slider back. Two things the panel says and means: assemble a character with a body first, and if a control rig (§6) is standing over the character, remove it before reshaping and build it again afterwards.
docs.title: 5. Proportions

docs.text: The character's own skeleton — 1212 joints — which any body rig is built over. The same character on the rig the one click builds. This is the port's own feature. The Blender add-on rigs with Rigify ; Maya has mGear , and a MetaHuman user already has it installed — so the click places mGear's own MetaHuman guide on the character's joints and builds mGear's Shifter rig over it. Put mGear's scripts folder on MAYA_MODULE_PATH first. Then, in the main panel's mGear Rig (Maya-only) frame: Button What it does One-Click mGear Rig snap the guide onto the character, build the rig, and bind the head Snap mGear Guide put the guide's locators back on the joints, for a guide you moved by hand Bind Head to mGear Rig constrain the head part to the body joints mGear drives (the one-click does this already) Unbind Head from mGear Rig take those constraints out again; the head keeps its values where it stands Register Anim Picker make mGear's Anim Picker for the rig — body and face pages — and open it Remove mGear Rig delete the guide and the rigs; the character stays as it is Two details the plug-in reports rather than hides: a guide locator whose joint the character does not have is left where the template put it (and the console says which), and a MetaHuman is two skeletons that share joint names — the neck's, among others — so the other part's joints are given names of their own while mGear connects and their own names back afterwards.
docs.title: 6. The body rig — mGear, one click

docs.text: The Rigify Body Control Rig frame in the main panel is the add-on's rig workflow, and in Maya it builds a Maya control rig over the character's key joints (the add-on's two steps, 1. Build Meta-Rig and 2. Generate Control Rig , then 3. Apply Retarget so the character follows it). Alongside them: Remove Retarget / Remove Control Rig take it back out; Link Head Rig / Unlink Head Rig attach the head part, which is what makes the face follow the body; Toggle RBF Correctives (Body) , Driver Bone , Show RBF Controls / Hide — the add-on's RBF corrective pass and its manual controls; Import FBX Animation… imports animation onto the rig; Toggle IK Stretch , Toggle Heel Pivot , Toggle Finger IK , IK to FK / FK to IK , Snap Fingertip Targets — the limb and finger switches, including the per-finger 0 = joints, 1 = fingertip blend. Retargeting an animation from another rig is its own panel — §15.
docs.title: The add-on's own rig buttons

docs.text: Several bodies averaged into one new character. A source row is either a body DNA file (with the head DNA that goes with it) or one archetype of a library file, and each has a weight. One row is the primary — the highlighted one — and it has to be a real DNA file, because a library entry carries no RigLogic data of its own: the primary is what the new character's rig is built from. Use Base DNA adds the bundled reference Body.dna (and Head.dna ) as the primary row; Add Body DNA / Add Folder… add files at weight 0 ; Load Library… adds a library's archetypes at 0 ; Export… writes a library file out. Build Blended Body averages the rows that carry weight — body and, when every one of them has head data, head too — and builds a new character in the slot list. Blend Active Character applies the blend to the character you already have instead, and Replace chooses between adding and replacing. Live Preview is off by default: it is the switch that makes a weight drag show its result while you drag.
docs.title: 7. Body Blend

docs.text: Import Clothing (FBX)… brings a garment in (and Head Accessory… the same for something that goes on the head). Make Garment Rig , then Bind Garment To Character — binding copies the body's skin weights onto the piece, so it moves the way the skin beneath it moves. Fit to the skin keeps a garment out of the character's body. A garment modelled over another build sinks into this one wherever the two differ; the fit finds, for every vertex, the nearest point of the body and head skin, and one that is inside it - or closer than the offset - is moved out along the skin's normal. Nothing else moves, so loose cloth stays loose, and a point that only slides along the skin is left alone. Fit Clothing to Skin (the Fit to Skin frame) fits the selected garment - or everything worn when nothing is selected. It also runs by itself on Bind Garment To Character and on Refit . Clothing Offset (0–0.02, the add-on's metres: 0.01 is one centimetre) is the gap left between cloth and skin; the minimum is 0.2 cm, and moving the slider refits what is worn straight away. The fit always starts from the garment as it was first seen, so a smaller offset lets the cloth come back out. A point deeper than 8 cm inside the skin is taken for another surface (an arm behind the torso) and is not pulled across. On a skinned garment the fit is written to the rest shape the skin cluster reads, so it stays when the character moves. Refit Clothing To Body re-applies the proportions' girth field to everything worn, so a changed waist changes the clothes over it too - and then fits the result to the skin with the Clothing Offset. Hair is a separate road, and it is an XGen interactive groom : Import Hair… (Alembic) reads the file as data and makes one XGen spline description on the character's head mesh - no node per strand (a MetaHuman groom has hundreds of thousands, which is what took Maya down when the file was imported the ordinary way). The groom's Z-up is turned to Maya's Y-up. Import chooses Guides + Strands , Strands only or Guides only . A file written by a groom exporter marks each curve ( groom_guide ), so the three really differ; a file without that mark is all strands. Hair Strands (0 = all) limits how many are built. XGen evaluates about 1.4 ms a strand, so the default of 10,000 is a few seconds; raise it for a finished groom. Line it up by eye. XGen holds a groom's own node at identity, so moving it does nothing. The import gives a locator, MMB_Hair_…_move , and a light preview of 250 strands under it: drag it and the preview follows at once. Nothing is written on release - the placement is applied by the press that seats the groom ( Bind , Retarget , Apply Hair Offset / Scale ), so lining hair up stays a drag and not a wait. Picking the hair picks the locator for you. Align Active Mesh to DNA Head seats the groom's roots on the head's surface : the mean vector from each root to the nearest point of the character mesh, iterated, all three axes of it, and the answer carries the measurement (the roots' mean and worst distance to the surface, before and after). It used to be a bounding box - the groom's control centred on the character mesh's box in X and Z, the height left alone - and measured on the sample guide groom over the bundled body that took the roots further from the head: 13.23 units off the surface before the button, 17.34 after. The surface fit takes the same groom, deliberately slid by (12, 15, -9) , from 20.14 back to 2.52 - and a groom that is already seated is left alone, because a step is only taken when it measures better. Hair Offset X/Y/Z , Hair Scale and Apply Hair Offset / Scale place it by number instead, and the numbers are absolute : the button puts the locator at the groom's own centre plus the offset (uniform scale from Hair Scale ) and writes the file in that same press, so it does not add to a hand drag - a groom lined up by eye returns to centre plus offset. What that buys is repeatability: the same numbers give the same placement in any scene. Bind Hair To Head re-seats the groom on the head mesh, so it follows the skin and Body Blend (a hair mesh or curves are constrained to the head joint instead). The light strand display the import made stays - it is the visible hair, and it is moved onto the head joint with the rest, so it follows the skin too. (It used to be deleted here, which is why the curves seemed to vanish on bind.) Retarget Hair to Selected Mesh does the same onto another mesh: select the hair, then the mesh. Sculpt brushes (Comb, Grab, Length, Smooth…) work on the groom. Density and Place are a different matter : they paint how strands are generated , and an imported groom is the file's own strands - measured, its density mask, its multiplier and its interpolation move 2745 splines not at all, and two renders of the same frame differ in 0 of 864000 bytes. There is no XGen grooming conversion, and the panel no longer offers one. Maya 2027 cannot turn an Alembic groom into XGen's own spline or guide data: the only ABC path is a spline modifier that streams the file ( xgmCurveToSpline ), so the description holds no splines of its own and the ABC has to travel with the scene. Measured here: the reader keeps the file open, and Epic's own groom exporter refuses a spline description ( Must select either palette or description ) - it is built for classic descriptions only, and that path crashed this Maya in the batch test. The buttons that grew a second, classic description out of the curves ( Create XGen Groom , Apply Hair Length , Apply Hair Width , Write Groom Collection , Bake Hair for Render ) were therefore taken out of the panel: they did not convert the imported hair, they made a different one. What the port does instead is what XGen supports - import, place, bind, and groom with the interactive brushes, whose edits are sculpt layers on top of the file's splines. Place first, bind once. Dragging MMB_Hair_…_move moves the stand-in curves only; the groom's Alembic is written by the press that says where it belongs - Bind Hair To Head , Retarget Hair to Selected Mesh , Apply Hair Offset / Scale or Align Active Mesh to DNA Head . Those place the groom where it was dragged and then seat it. Re-writing the file on every drag release was the seconds-long stall the stand-in was invented for. Deleting the character takes its hair with it. An imported groom is a scene root of its own - XGen makes it beside the mesh, and the placement locator beside that - so removing a character used to leave the groom, its locator and its 250 stand-in curves floating over nothing. The character's record now carries its hair, so all three go with it.
docs.title: 8. Wearables — clothing and hair

docs.text: The add-on's workflow, translated: sculpt the skin in a pose, and keep the difference as a named corrective that comes back with that pose. Name the corrective ( Corrective ), and give it the bone it hangs off for a face ( Head Bone ) or a body ( Body Driver Bone ) pass. Begin (Face) or Begin (Body) takes a baseline: the mesh as it stands and the pose that stands with it. Sculpt the vertices — the port's delta is taken against that baseline. Finish Sculpt stores the difference, sparse and named, on the character. Edit Sculpt loads a stored corrective back for another pass, Set Neutral re-keys the pose it hangs off, Toggle Manual Override marks it always-on, and Remove Corrective deletes it. Sync to Wearables carries the applied difference onto worn garments through the same nearest-vertex map the garment bind uses. Bake Corrective to DNA writes it into the DNA file; Write to DNA (head only) ( Export Edited Shape Keys ) and Bake All to DNA do the same for a batch. A DNA key you sculpted yourself — jaw_open , say — replaces that channel when you press Export Edited Shape Keys . Export… and Import… move the whole registry as JSON. The deltas are the data; everything else in the panel is bookkeeping around them.
docs.title: 9. Live corrective sculpting (Beta)

docs.text: Head and Body write the active slot's DNA, through the library's own writer, read back as proof. Export FBX writes the character through the FBX plug-in; Export glTF through Maya's glTF translator. With no path given, a file dialog asks. The Save Head / Save Body DNA commands are the same two files with a suggested name — <source stem>_export.dna , beside the DNA it was read from — and with the Include Mesh Edits question answered: what Proportions (§5) and Sculpt (§9) did lives on the Maya skeleton and mesh, and the writer patches those edits into the file the character came from, so the DNA is the character on screen. Lower LODs follow the nearest LOD-0 vertex, or they would keep the unedited shape and pop in the distance. If the mesh edits cannot be written, the port says so loudly instead of writing a file that quietly dropped them. Export All Slots (§11) does the DNA export for every slot in the list.
docs.title: 10. Exporting

docs.text: Validate DNA File… reads a .dna and reports what is wrong with it; Validate Active Slot does the same for the character you are working on, so a file that will not assemble is a sentence before the pipeline meets it rather than a stack trace later. Batch Tools is two buttons: Assemble All Characters (every character in the folder the plug-in is pointed at) and Export All Slots (the DNA of every slot in the scene).
docs.title: 11. DNA validation and batch tools

docs.text: Plain files in one shared folder , and the plug-in that ships in mmb/md_plugin . Maya → MD: Send Body to MD writes an avatar .obj into the shared folder ( Send Scale , Include Head and Prepare for Auto-Fit decide what goes in it). In Marvelous Designer, add the scripts from the plug-in folder in Plug-in > Plug-in Manager — maya_live.py for Live , and maya_load_avatar.py / maya_send_garment.py for a one-shot round trip — and run the one you need. Open MD Plug-in Folder opens that folder for you. MD → Maya: the garment lands in the same folder. Get Garment Now imports the newest one, Import Garment from MD… picks a file by hand, and Live watches the folder on idle and imports the moment a garment lands, so the round trip is one click on each side. Buttons and zippers are dropped, the avatar and lean copies are excluded, and units are honoured through the plug-in's own .mayaunits.json . Merge Pattern Pieces chooses between the patterns as cut and one welded mesh; Wear As is the category the garment is worn as, and Sim Steps / Auto Return tune what the round trip does.
docs.title: 12. MD Live — Marvelous Designer

docs.text: Two localhost ports, MetaBridge Live's own: 9584 receives characters and poses, 9586 is the live link. They are not the ports any other Cascadeur bridge uses, so it can run beside one. Nothing leaves the machine. Press Install Cascadeur Plug-in once. The plug-in - MetaBridge Live , two files - ships in third_party/MetaBridgeLive ; Cascadeur keeps its scripts inside its own installation, which usually needs Administrator rights — the installer does the copy through a short-lived helper and reports what happened, and says so when the prompt is refused rather than half-installing. Choose what to send: Send ( Character and Bones or Keyframes Only ), Send Head , Face Bones , Send Anim , Append , Frame Rate . Press Send to Cascadeur (the whole scene, opens as a new scene in Cascadeur) or Current Frame (one frame, over the top from frame 0). Restart Cascadeur, then run Animation Scripts > MetaBridge Live once per session (run it again to stop). Cascadeur Status answers whether it is listening. Live: Mirror This Rig sends frames while you animate, and Stop Mirroring stops; Live Way and Live Bones choose what a mirrored frame carries. Send the character first, then go live. Clothes go with the character. Every mesh skinned to the character's joints (what Bind Garment recorded, and anything else bound to the rig) leaves in the same FBX and follows the pose in Cascadeur. A garment is re-skinned on a copy from the body and the head under it - so a hood follows the head and a baggy leg follows its own leg - and the original is not touched; the head's own neck and shoulder collar takes the body's weights, so the head stays joined at the neck. Send the character in its rest pose and let the pose follow (a character sent while posed can tear its clothes in Cascadeur). A coat with 170,000 vertices takes about half a minute. The character leaves as one skeleton - the head part's meshes are rebound to its body joints - and a take read back lands on both parts: the head's own copy of the body chain ( spine_04 up to head , the clavicles and the upperarms, at the body's exact rest transforms) is written from the body joints of the same name, so the head and its face ride along instead of standing in their rest pose. A character with no head part beside it is unaffected, and so is the face itself, which keeps being driven by the DNA's rig logic.
docs.title: 13. Send to Cascadeur

docs.text: Out (9561) — press Open Unreal Plug-in Folder once; it fetches MotionForgeLiveLink from GitHub the first time, and you copy it into your project's Plugins folder and restart the editor. In Unreal's Live Link window add the MotionForge source (port 9561); in the character Blueprint keep Use Live Link off . Then Start Unreal Live streams the face as you work — the same RigLogic runs on both sides, so only control values cross, one small frame per tick at the Rate you set. Mirror chooses what the stream carries. In (9562) — Follow Unreal makes this character follow a MetaHuman Unreal is animating: Host , Port , Rate , Body and Face decide what follows, and each frame's per-joint turns and offsets are applied as a delta from the rest pose captured when the follow began — and put back when it stops. Run MotionForge.Send.Start in Unreal first.
docs.title: 14. Unreal Engine

docs.text: Animation Baker — keyframe the face board's controls, then Bake Face Animation over the frame range; Clear Baked Animation takes the bake out again. (The panel's own line says the order: key the board first, then bake.) Pose Reset — Reset All Controls puts the whole face board back to neutral, Reset Selected only the controls you have selected, which is the one you want in the middle of a pose. External Preset Converter — a foreign preset names bones ; the board names controls , so the two are matched through a name_mapping.json . Convert & Import (Maya/Houdini)… brings a preset in from those tools and Convert ARKit Payload… from an ARKit payload; Edit Name Mapping opens the mapping to fill the empty targets before a re-import. Retarget Rigify Animation — bring animation from another rig onto this character. Source Type picks the profile — fifteen of them, from Auto Detect , UE5 Mannequin , Fortnite , MetaHuman , Mixamo and Rigify to SMPL-X , SOMA and Unitree G1 — Source Rig / Target Rig point at the two rigs, and Quality chooses the solve: Precise (floor + legs on IK) , Balanced (legs on IK) or Fast (rotations only) . Under the add-on's rows is the port's own frame, Retarget in Maya (HumanIK / mGear) , and it is where the take lands: Retarget Onto — the character's own joints (the solve keyed on the character's skeleton: rest poses aligned, root travel scaled, feet on IK, floor matched), HumanIK (Maya) (both rigs defined as HIK characters and Maya's own retarget baked), or the one-click mGear Controls . Target Type picks which rig on the character side the solve uses, Legs on IK keeps the feet on the floor rather than rotating them, and Source Rest Frame is the frame of the source take that stands as the rest pose ( -1 lets the solver work it out).
docs.title: 15. Animation baker, pose reset, preset converter, retarget

docs.text: Anything a panel does, a command does. Every button is a Maya runtime command: cmds.mmb_mh_assemble() from the Script Editor, a MEL script or a shelf button. Maya's own tooltip on a button says which add-on feature it stands for and whether the work behind it is ported; the command's own name is beside each button in the Panel Reference . Settings are optionVars , prefixed mmb. , named after the add-on's property (the Textures checkbox is mmb.ml_mh_load_textures ). They survive a restart and can be set from MEL: optionVar -iv "mmb.ml_mh_load_textures" 0; From Python , mmb.api is the facade: import mmb.api as api api . status () # how much of the add-on is ported api . panels () # the eighteen panels, in sidebar order api . window () # open the hub api . run ( "mmb_mh_assemble" ) # run one button - Batch hosts : anything that needs a window refuses in mayapy and says so; the work that does not — assembling, exporting to a path you give, validating, baking — runs there, which is how the port's own test suite runs it ( tests/run_tests.py ). - Nothing is hidden in the scene : a character is a group of ordinary joints and meshes, the slot list is one network node ( MMB_Slots ) holding the data, and every setting is an optionVar — so a scene saved by the plug-in opens in any Maya, with or without the plug-in loaded.
docs.title: Quick tips

docs.text: 124 of the add-on's 143 commands are implemented. The 19 that are not are the 18 panel ids (the add-on's panel classes, which have no Maya counterpart — the port draws its own windows) and mmb_save_mat_defaults , Save Material as Default : it would capture Blender's Principled BSDF socket values, and the port's materials are Arnold standardSurface nodes whose attribute names are entirely different — and nothing in the port reads such a file yet, so writing one would be a button that produces a file nobody reads. (Reload Materials and Reset Material Defaults are there and work.)* The plug-in's own checking happens out loud : a command that cannot do its work prints why in the Script Editor and, where it can, says it in the viewport, rather than changing nothing. The Cascadeur elevated install — the copy into a Program Files Cascadeur — is implemented and its planning half is tested, but the elevation half has not been run against a real installation of that kind. Report what happens if you use it. This guide's screenshots come from Maya 2027 on Windows, with the reference MetaHuman. Menu wording and window decoration differ on other systems; the panels are the same panels.
